Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.
Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single Spring Boot web application backed by an Oracle database. The application serves gallery pages and photo content directly, with no gateway or external service integrations identified.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Client Layer"] Browser["Web Browser"] end subgraph App["Application Layer - Spring Boot 2.7.18"] Web["Spring MVC and Thymeleaf"] Security["Spring Security HTTP Basic"] Service["Photo Business Service"] Data["Spring Data JPA and Hibernate"] end subgraph Storage["Data Layer"] Oracle[("Oracle Database")] end Browser -->|"HTTP requests"| Security Security -->|"authorized requests"| Web Web -->|"photo operations"| Service Service -->|"repository calls"| Data Data -->|"JDBC queries and BLOBs"| Oracle Oracle -->|"photo records"| Data

LayerTechnologyVersionPurpose
PresentationSpring MVC and ThymeleafSpring Boot 2.7.18; Thymeleaf 3.0.15.RELEASEServer-rendered gallery and detail pages; upload and photo responses
ApplicationJava8Photo upload, retrieval, navigation, and deletion logic
SecuritySpring Security5.7.11HTTP Basic authentication on state-changing requests
PersistenceSpring Data JPA and Hibernate2.7.18 / 5.6.15.FinalRepository and ORM access
DatabaseOracle Database Freegvenzl/oracle-free:latest in ComposePhoto metadata and binary image storage
Runtime packagingDocker ComposeNot pinnedRuns the application and Oracle database containers

Data Storage & External Services

Photo records and image bytes are stored in Oracle as a relational entity with BLOB content. There is no cache, message broker, object-storage provider, or external API integration identified; the only separately deployed dependency is the Oracle database container.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Uses a layered MVC → service → Spring Data repository pattern.
  • Stores image bytes in the database rather than on a file system or object store.
  • Uses Oracle-specific native SQL for photo navigation, reporting, and pagination.

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application exposes five HTTP routes: server-rendered gallery/detail pages, a multipart upload operation, a photo-byte response, and a delete operation. Requests are handled synchronously within one application process; no inter-service API calls or asynchronous messaging were found.

DTOs & Contracts

Photo is the service-level JPA entity used to represent a persisted photo and returned to server-rendered views. UploadResult is a mutable POJO used internally between the service and upload controller. The upload request is Spring's multipart file contract; the controller assembles a mutable Map response rather than a dedicated response DTO. No immutable records, gateway aggregation DTOs, protobuf/GraphQL schemas, or explicit OpenAPI documents were found. Spring Boot's Jackson support is present for JSON serialization.

Communication Patterns

Controllers call the PhotoService interface synchronously; PhotoServiceImpl calls PhotoRepository, which uses Spring Data JPA/Hibernate and JDBC to access Oracle. There are no message brokers, asynchronous handlers, circuit breakers, retry policies, API gateway, or service discovery client. Docker Compose uses the logical hostname oracle-db for database connectivity. Database readiness gates application startup through Compose depends_on: condition: service_healthy; application readiness has no separately configured health endpoint. Authentication is HTTP Basic for /upload and /detail/*/delete; other requests are public. TLS/HTTPS is not configured in the repository, and CSRF is disabled for the stateless security configuration.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Oracle database starts and runs its internal healthcheck.sh every 30 seconds (10-second timeout, 15 retries, 180-second start period).

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets users upload images, browse a shared gallery, inspect image metadata, navigate between photos, and delete records. The primary domain is a single photo collection rather than multiple user-owned albums or service-specific bounded contexts.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhoto Album / Photo GalleryAn uploaded image and the metadata needed to display, retrieve, navigate, and remove itEach photo is an independent gallery item; no other domain entity is modeled
UploadResultPhoto Album / Upload ProcessingResult of an individual upload attempt, including success or failure informationProduced by the upload service and consumed by the upload controller; not persisted

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
Photo AlbumPhoto Gallery and Upload ManagementPhoto records; transient UploadResult responsesOracle database for persistent photo records and image bytes

The application is a monolith with a shared Oracle schema. No cross-service domain exchange or separate source-of-truth boundary was found.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload Photos

  1. A client submits files through POST /upload.
  2. HomeController delegates each file to PhotoServiceImpl.uploadPhoto.
  3. The service checks the declared MIME type, configured per-file size limit, non-empty content, and image dimensions (up to 40 million pixels when a reader recognizes the image).
  4. Accepted bytes and metadata are persisted as a Photo record in Oracle; rejected items are returned as failed upload results.
  5. The controller collects successful and failed results into a JSON response. An empty file list receives HTTP 400; per-file validation failures are included in a normal upload response.

Workflow 2: Browse and Navigate Photos

  1. A client opens the gallery page at GET /; the controller retrieves photos ordered newest first and renders the gallery.
  2. Selecting a photo opens GET /detail/{id}. The application loads the record and requests older/newer records for navigation.
  3. Photo content is retrieved separately through GET /photo/{id}, which returns the database BLOB with the persisted MIME type.
  4. Missing IDs or missing image bytes result in a redirect or not-found response, depending on the request.

Workflow 3: Delete a Photo

  1. An authenticated client submits POST /detail/{id}/delete.
  2. The service finds the photo by ID and deletes the entity from Oracle.
  3. The controller redirects to the gallery with a success or not-found message; unexpected errors are logged and surfaced as a generic failure message.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no cross-service data composition or gateway aggregation flows. The Photo Album application is the only business service and reads/writes its photo data directly through the repository to Oracle. Compose waits for the database container's health check before starting the application, but there is no runtime service-to-service fallback behavior.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Gallery User" participant Web as "Photo Album Web" participant Service as "Photo Service" participant Repo as "Photo Repository" participant DB as "Oracle Database" User->>Web: Upload image Web->>Service: Validate and store submitted file Service->>Service: Check MIME type, size, non-empty content, and dimensions alt File accepted Service->>Repo: Save Photo and image bytes Repo->>DB: Persist photo record and BLOB DB-->>Repo: Stored photo Repo-->>Service: Saved Photo Service-->>Web: Upload success Web-->>User: Show successful upload result else File rejected or persistence fails Service-->>Web: Upload failure result Web-->>User: Show failure details end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • The configured MIME allowlist is JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP; the service also checks the configured 10 MiB file limit and rejects empty files.
  • If an image reader identifies dimensions, uploads exceeding 40 million pixels are rejected; unrecognized image content can proceed without dimensions.
  • Each stored photo receives a generated UUID-based identifier and a generated storage filename; original filename and MIME type are retained as metadata.
  • Gallery results are ordered by upload time. Detail navigation queries for photos before and after the current upload timestamp.
  • Upload and deletion service methods operate transactionally. Spring Security requires HTTP Basic authentication for upload and deletion; gallery reads remain public.
  • No multi-step compensation, event-driven workflow, audit trail, or explicit lifecycle state machine was identified.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The project uses Spring Boot 2.7.18 and Java 8, both older platform baselines. Dependency advisory analysis identified vulnerabilities in resolved dependencies; detailed medium-and-higher findings are recorded in the security assessment. Commons IO is explicitly pinned to 2.11.0 while most Spring versions are parent-managed.

Notable Observations

  • The Spring Boot parent manages most direct and transitive versions; the parent is not separately counted among the 11 declared dependencies.
  • Oracle JDBC is runtime-scoped; H2 is test-scoped, so the test database differs from production.
  • The resolved dependency tree contains 73 compile, 2 runtime, and 26 test-scope coordinates (101 total).

Caching Strategy

No application cache provider, cache annotations, cache regions, or second-level Hibernate cache configuration was detected. Photo reads are served from repository/database operations; the gallery adds a timestamp for browser cache busting, not server-side data caching.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The single application owns all photo records in one Oracle schema. There are no service-isolated stores, cross-service queries, CQRS projections, or cross-service aggregation flows. The test profile substitutes an in-memory H2 database and does not provide production Oracle behavior parity for Oracle-specific native SQL.
